title: Methods that use methods
summary: scaleJoystick calls clamp; isPalindrome calls reverseString.

say.never: `cubeOf` needs the same squaring that `squareOf` already does. Instead of copying it, we **call** `squareOf` from inside. Methods can use other methods, just like you can ask a friend for help instead of redoing their job.
say.bit: `cubeOf` calls `squareOf` instead of repeating its code.

steps.title: In your lesson: Don't repeat yourself

say.never: `scaleJoystick` needs the same range check that `clamp` already does. Instead of copying it, we **call** `clamp` from inside. Methods can use other methods, just like you can ask a friend for help instead of redoing their job.
say.bit: `scaleJoystick` needs the same range check `clamp` already does, so it **calls** clamp instead of copying it.

say.never: Build on what you have. `greetLoudly` doesn't write its own shouting code. It builds a greeting and hands it to `shout`, which we already wrote. Small methods that do one job become building blocks for bigger ones.
say.bit: Build bigger methods from small ones: `greetLoudly` reuses `shout`.

steps.title: In your lesson: Build on what you have

say.never: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like "racecar". So the test is: *is the word equal to its own reverse?* We already wrote `reverseString`, so we just call it.
say.bit: A palindrome reads the same backwards, so: does it equal its own reverse?

say.never: If the range check ever needs to change, you fix it in **one** place and everything that calls it gets the fix. That's the big reason methods exist.
say.bit: If the range check ever changes, you fix it in **one** place, and every caller gets the fix. That's the whole point of methods.
